pos: adj. and v. (walled, defended, hedged about — in the KJV the standing word for a fortified city, for a planted vineyard, and for the frame of a man's body)
etymology: From Middle English fensen, a shortening of defensen, to defend; so a fence is a defence before it is a boundary. The KJV uses it to render several Hebrew words for walling, hedging, and cutting off.
biblical_def: Fenced in the Authorized Version means fortified, and it is used in three registers that repay attention. Militarily it describes the walled towns of Canaan and Judah: “All these cities were fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many” (Deu 3:5), and the terrible sentence of Hezekiah's fourteenth year, when Sennacherib “come up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them” (2Ki 18:13) — every fortification in the kingdom fell, and Jerusalem was spared not by its walls but by an angel. Agriculturally it describes God's labour on His vineyard: “he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine” (Isa 5:2), and the whole tragedy of that song is that the vineyard, given everything, brought forth wild grapes — whereupon the LORD says He will take away the hedge and break down the wall. And anatomically, in the most surprising use of all, Job says of his own frame: “Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews” (Job 10:11). The body is a walled city. In every register the point is the same: what is fenced is fenced by another, and stands only while He maintains the wall.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fenced as enclosed with a fence, guarded, fortified; and fence as a wall, hedge or enclosure raised to defend, from the verb to fend or defend.
webster_full: FENCED, pp. Enclosed with a fence; guarded; fortified.
FENCE, n. That which defends; a wall, hedge, ditch, bank, or line of posts and rails, raised for the security of enclosed ground.
A fenced city, in Scripture, is a city surrounded with a wall, in distinction from an unwalled town or village.
The word is a contraction of defence, from the verb to fend, to keep off.
FENCE, v.t. To enclose with a hedge, wall or other barrier; to guard; to fortify.
scriptures: Deu 3:5
All these cities were fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many.
Now in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah did Sennacherib king of Assyria come up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them.
Isa 5:2

And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.
Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews.
corruption_summary: Security is sought in the fence — the wall, the policy, the reserve fund — when Scripture makes the fence itself a gift held at God's pleasure, removable in a single season.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Scripture consistently does with fortifications. Judah had a whole system of fenced cities, and in one campaign Sennacherib took every one of them. Isaiah's vineyard had a hedge and a wall, and the judgment announced is simply their removal: “I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down” (Isa 5:5). The Bible is not against walls — Nehemiah built one and it was a work of God — but it will not let a man rest in one. “Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1).

Job 10:11 is the sentence to carry away. A man's own body is described as a fortification God built — skin and flesh for the covering, bones and sinews for the wall — and Job says it in the middle of an argument about why God is now pulling it down. The doctrine of creation reaches all the way into the frame: “I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psa 139:14), which forbids both the contempt for the body that gnosticism teaches and the worship of it that the present age teaches. And the same hand that fenced it will one day take the fence down, and raise it again incorruptible.
roots_summary: English fence, from defence; rendering Hebrew batsar (H1219), to cut off, make inaccessible, fortify; suk (H7753), to hedge about; 'azaq (H5823), to dig about.
roots_lines: Hebrew batsar (H1219) — to cut off, enclose, fortify; the word behind “fenced cities”.
Hebrew mibtsar (H4013) — a fortress, stronghold; the noun from the same root.
Hebrew suk (H7753) — to hedge, fence about; used of the hedge Satan complains God set around Job (Job 1:10).
Hebrew 'azaq (H5823) — to dig about, fence in; the verb of Isa 5:2.
Hebrew sakak (H5526) — to cover, screen, hedge in; used of God covering David in the day of battle (Psa 140:7).
usage: “Fenced with high walls, gates, and bars” — the cities of the land.
“He fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof” — God's labour on His vineyard.
“Hast fenced me with bones and sinews” — the body as a walled city.

pos: v. (pitched a camp, lodged in tents — the verb of Israel's forty years, and of the angel of the LORD around those who fear Him)
etymology: From French encamper, from en, in, and camp, from Latin campus, a field. The KJV uses it chiefly for Hebrew chanah, to decline or bend down — the picture is of pitching a tent by lowering oneself to the ground.
biblical_def: Encamped is the verb of the wilderness. It first appears at the very start of the journey — “they took their journey from Succoth, and encamped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness” (Exo 13:20) — and it recurs at every stage of Numbers 33, a chapter that is nothing but a list of forty years of removing and pitching. The word carries no permanence in it. Israel encamped and struck camp at the moving of a cloud, and the arrangement of the camp itself was a sermon: the tabernacle in the centre, the Levites round about it, and the twelve tribes by their standards outside them (Num 1:50) — God in the midst of His people, guarded by His ministers. The word also marks the two extremities of the exodus: Israel encamped by the sea and “the Egyptians pursued after them… and overtook them encamping by the sea” (Exo 14:9); and at rest, “they came to Elim, where were twelve wells of water, and threescore and ten palm trees: and they encamped there by the waters” (Exo 15:27). At the end of the wandering the same verb signals arrival: “the children of Israel encamped in Gilgal, and kept the passover… in the plains of Jericho” (Jos 5:10). And once, gloriously, it is God who does the encamping: “The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him” (Psa 34:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines encamp as to pitch tents, to form and occupy a camp; and encamped as settled in a camp, or lodged in tents.
webster_full: ENCAMP, v.i. To pitch tents or form huts, as an army; to halt on a march and place in temporary habitations for the night.
To take up a position, as an army or company.
ENCAMP, v.t. To form into a camp; to place a marching army or company in a temporary habitation.
ENCAMPED, pp. Settled in a camp; having taken a temporary station.
The Israelites encamped by the wells of water in the wilderness.
scriptures: And they took their journey from Succoth, and encamped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness.
And they came to Elim, where were twelve wells of water, and threescore and ten palm trees: and they encamped there by the waters.
Jos 5:10
And the children of Israel encamped in Gilgal, and kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the month at even in the plains of Jericho.
Psa 34:7
The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.
corruption_summary: Rootlessness is celebrated as freedom and settlement despised, or the reverse; Scripture makes the camp a temporary obedience to a moving cloud, with the destination fixed and not chosen.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the rhythm of the word. Israel did not encamp where it liked or move when it wearied of a place; it moved when the cloud was taken up and pitched when the cloud rested, “whether it was by day or by night” (Num 9:21). Two temptations attend the Christian life and the camp rebukes both: the settler who drives his tent-pegs so deep he cannot follow, and the wanderer who calls his restlessness a pilgrimage. The camp is provisional and the destination is not negotiable.

The second thing worth holding is the shape of the camp, because it is theology in canvas. The tabernacle stood in the middle, the tribe of Levi encamped round about it as a cordon, and the twelve tribes pitched outside by their standards — and Num 1:53 gives the reason for the cordon plainly: “that there be no wrath upon the congregation.” Nearness to a holy God is a mercy and a danger at once, and the ministry stood in between. That arrangement is fulfilled and transfigured in Christ, who “dwelt among us” — the Greek of Joh 1:14 is literally that He tabernacled, pitched His tent, among us — and who is Himself the Priest that makes nearness safe.
roots_summary: Latin campus, a field; rendering Hebrew chanah (H2583), to decline, pitch a tent, encamp; machaneh (H4264), a camp; Greek parembole (G3925).
roots_lines: Hebrew chanah (H2583) — to bend down, pitch a tent, encamp; the root of the name Hannah, grace.
Hebrew machaneh (H4264) — a camp, host, company; Jacob named Mahanaim, two camps, from it (Gen 32:2).
Hebrew nasa' (H5265) — to pull up stakes, to journey; the paired verb of Numbers 33.
Hebrew degel (H1714) — a standard, banner; each tribe pitched by its own (Num 2:2).
Greek parembole (G3925) — a camp; “let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp” (Heb 13:13).
usage: “Encamped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness” — the first stage of forty years.
“They encamped there by the waters” — Elim, twelve wells and seventy palms.
“The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him” — a camp with a guard.

pos: n. pl. (traders, dealers in wares carried between countries — honoured in Proverbs, indicted in the prophets, and weeping at the fall of Babylon)
etymology: From Old French marchant, from Latin mercari, to trade, from merx, merchandise. The Hebrew words rendered merchant are chiefly socher, one who travels about, and rokel, a pedlar or trafficker; and Kena'an, Canaan, is itself used to mean a trafficker.
biblical_def: Scripture is not squeamish about merchants. The virtuous woman of Pro 31 is praised in their terms — “She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar” (Pro 31:14) — and she buys a field, plants a vineyard, and makes fine linen and sells it. Trade is a lawful calling and a mark of a functioning society. But Scripture also watches what trade does to a people when it becomes the whole of their life. Tyre is the case study: “the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth” (Isa 23:8), and Ezekiel's lament over her runs for three chapters and ends in the sea. Nehemiah found the sabbath being eroded exactly where one would expect — “the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice” (Neh 13:20), camping at the gates until he threatened to lay hands on them. And the Revelation gives the last word: when Babylon falls, “the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more” (Rev 18:11), and the cargo list that follows ends with an item that indicts the whole trade — “slaves, and souls of men”.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a merchant as one who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who buys and sells goods for profit.
webster_full: MERCHANT, n. A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods and sells them by wholesale.
In popular usage, any trader, or one who deals in the purchase and sale of goods.
MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.
The word is from the French marchand, and ultimately from the Latin mercor, to buy.
In Scripture the merchants of Tyre are called princes, and the merchants of the earth are said to weep at the fall of Babylon.
scriptures: She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar.
Isa 23:8
Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth?
So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice.
And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:
corruption_summary: Commerce is either sanctified without qualification or condemned as such; Scripture blesses honest trade, forbids the false balance, and reserves its judgment for the traffic that finally deals in souls of men.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors face each other here and both are common in the church. The first baptises commerce entire, treating profit as self-evidently the fruit of virtue and the market as a moral arbiter. Scripture will not: it legislates against the false balance as an abomination (Pro 11:1), forbids interest taken from a poor brother, commands the corners of the field be left unreaped, and cancels debts every seventh year. The second error condemns trade as such and reads Rev 18 as a manifesto against enterprise. That will not stand either — Pro 31 makes a trading woman the model of a godly wife, and the Lord Jesus told parables in which the servant who traded and gained was commended and the one who buried the talent was condemned.

What Scripture actually indicts is a commerce that has become a religion, and it names the point at which the line is crossed. The merchandise of Babylon in Rev 18:12-13 is listed in descending order of luxury — gold, silver, precious stones, silk, scarlet, ivory, marble, cinnamon, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, beasts, sheep, horses, chariots — and the list ends “and slaves, and souls of men.” Human beings appear as the last line item of the inventory, which is precisely how a market that answers to nothing above itself will finally treat them. The traffic in persons is the terminus, and every age finds its own form of it.
roots_summary: Latin merx, merchandise; Hebrew socher (H5503), a traveller, trader; rokel (H7402), a pedlar; Kena'an (H3667), Canaan, also trafficker; Greek emporos (G1713).
roots_lines: Hebrew socher (H5503) — a merchant; from sachar, to go about, travel for trade.
Hebrew rokel (H7402) — a trafficker, pedlar; used repeatedly of Tyre in Eze 27.
Hebrew Kena'an (H3667) — Canaan; the same word means a merchant, and Hos 12:7 puns on it.
Greek emporos (G1713) — a merchant, one on a journey for trade; the word of Rev 18:11 and of Mat 13:45.
Greek emporion (G1712) — a market-house; “make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” (Joh 2:16).
usage: “She is like the merchants' ships” — trade as a figure of a good wife's diligence.
“Whose merchants are princes” — Tyre at the height, and under sentence.
“The merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her” — the mourning of a lost market.

pos: n. pl. (shaped masses of baked bread — the units in which our Lord's two great feeding miracles are counted, and the thing the disciples kept failing to understand)
etymology: From Old English hlaf, bread — the same word behind lord (hlaford, loaf-ward) and lady (hlaefdige, loaf-kneader). The Greek is artos, a cake or loaf of bread, small and flat rather than the modern risen loaf.
biblical_def: Loaves is a counting word, and the Gospels count carefully. “We have here but five loaves, and two fishes” (Mat 14:17); John notes whose they were — “There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?” (Joh 6:9). Barley was the poor man's grain, and the loaves were small flat cakes; five of them and a boy's two dried fish fed five thousand men beside women and children, with twelve baskets over. Afterwards there were four thousand fed from seven, with seven baskets over. The numbers matter because the Lord Jesus later made an examination of them: “When I brake the five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? They say unto him, Twelve” (Mar 8:19), and having drawn out both totals He asked, “How is it that ye do not understand?” The disciples were at that moment anxious about having forgotten to bring bread. The word appears again in the parable of the friend at midnight — “Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luk 11:5) — the picture of importunate prayer; and in the loaves of shewbread that David ate, and in the one loaf broken at the last supper of which Paul says, “we being many are one bread, and one body”.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines loaf as a mass of bread when baked, and notes that the word originally signified simply bread.
webster_full: LOAF, n. plu. LOAVES. A mass of bread when baked; a mass or lump, as of sugar.
The word is the Saxon hlaf, bread; whence hlaford, a lord, that is, the giver of bread.
In Scripture the loaves were small and flat cakes, commonly of barley or of wheat.
Five barley loaves and two small fishes were multiplied to feed five thousand men.
The shewbread consisted of twelve cakes set in order upon the pure table before the Lord.
scriptures: And they say unto him, We have here but five loaves, and two fishes.
Joh 6:9
There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?
Mar 8:19
When I brake the five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? They say unto him, Twelve.
Luk 11:5
And he said unto them, Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say unto him, Friend, lend me three loaves;
corruption_summary: The feeding is explained away as a miracle of sharing — the crowd shamed into producing hidden lunches — which requires the evangelists to be mistaken about the one thing all four of them record.
corruption_paragraphs: The rationalising reading of the feeding of the five thousand has been in circulation since the early nineteenth century and is still preached: the boy's generosity moved the crowd to bring out food they had been hiding, and the real miracle was the sharing. It is worth naming what the reading costs. This is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels; John says the men counted five thousand and that the fragments filled twelve baskets; Mark preserves the Lord's own later interrogation of the disciples about the arithmetic; and the crowd's reaction was to try to take Him by force and make Him a king, which no picnic produces. A God who creates from nothing can multiply bread, and the sharing reading is not a humbler interpretation but a denial of the text by a writer who has decided in advance what may happen.

The rebuke in Mar 8 is the pastoral point and it is uncomfortable. The disciples, having twice watched Him feed thousands from almost nothing, were in a boat worrying that they had only one loaf with them. He asked them the numbers and they answered correctly — twelve baskets, seven baskets — and He said, “How is it that ye do not understand?” They had the data and not the deduction. That is the characteristic unbelief of a Christian who has been long in the way: not the denial of past mercies but the failure to reason from them, so that every new want finds the soul as bare as if nothing had ever been given.
roots_summary: Old English hlaf, bread; Greek artos (G740), a loaf of bread; Hebrew lechem (H3899), bread, food; kikkar lechem, a round loaf.
roots_lines: Greek artos (G740) — a loaf, bread; the word of “give us this day our daily bread” and of “I am the bread of life”.
Hebrew lechem (H3899) — bread, food generally; the second half of the name Bethlehem, house of bread.
Hebrew lechem hap-panim — the shewbread, literally “bread of the face”, twelve cakes before the LORD (Lev 24:5-6).
Greek krithinos (G2916) — of barley; the poor man's grain, specified only by John (Joh 6:9).
Greek klasma (G2801) — a fragment, broken piece; the leftovers gathered so that nothing be lost (Joh 6:12).
usage: “We have here but five loaves, and two fishes” — an inventory offered as an excuse.
“How many baskets full of fragments took ye up?” — an examination in remembering.
“Friend, lend me three loaves” — importunity at midnight.

pos: n. pl. (two distinct words in the KJV: the upright timbers of a doorway, and swift couriers who carry a king's letters)
etymology: Both senses come through Latin postis, a doorpost, and Latin positus, placed — a runner being one posted at a stage of the road. The KJV renders Hebrew mezuzah, a doorpost, and rats, a runner, by the same English word.
biblical_def: Posts in the Authorized Version means two unrelated things, and both are worth knowing. The first is the upright of a doorway, and it carries the blood of the passover: “they shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses, wherein they shall eat it” (Exo 12:7). Applied with hyssop, that blood was the difference between a house passed over and a house visited. The same posts carry the word: “thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates” (Deu 6:9) — the command from which the mezuzah comes. And in the temple, when Isaiah saw the LORD, “the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke” (Isa 6:4). Blood on the posts, the law on the posts, and the posts themselves shaking at the seraph's cry. The second sense is a courier: Hezekiah's invitation to a national passover went out this way — “so the posts went with the letters from the king and his princes throughout all Israel and Judah” (2Ch 30:6) — and Persia's riders carried both Haman's decree and its counter. Job uses them for the speed of a life: “my days are swifter than a post”.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives post both as a piece of timber set upright, especially the upright of a door, and as a courier or one who travels with speed to carry letters.
webster_full: POST, n. A piece of timber, metal or other solid substance, set upright, as the posts of a door or of a fence.
POST, n. A hasty messenger; a courier; one who travels expeditiously to carry letters or dispatches.
Hence, a station or stage where fresh horses were kept, whence the sense of the mail or post-office.
The blood of the passover lamb was struck on the two side posts and the upper door post.
The posts in the days of Ahasuerus rode upon mules and camels, hastened by the king's commandment.
scriptures: Exo 12:7
And they shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses, wherein they shall eat it.
Deu 6:9
And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.
Isa 6:4
And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke.

So the posts went with the letters from the king and his princes throughout all Israel and Judah, and according to the commandment of the king, saying, Ye children of Israel, turn again unto the LORD God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and he will return to the remnant of you, that are escaped out of the hand of the kings of Assyria.
corruption_summary: The blood on the posts is reduced to a token of belonging or a memorable ritual; the text says the destroyer passed over because of the blood, and the doctrine of substitution stands or falls there.
corruption_paragraphs: The doorpost of Exo 12 is one of the plainest pictures of penal substitution in Scripture, and it resists every softening. The Israelite household was not safe because it was Israelite; it was safe because a lamb without blemish had died in its place and the blood was where it could be seen. “When I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exo 12:13) — the ground is objective, external to the family's feelings, and applied. Modern treatments that make the atonement chiefly an example of self-giving love, or a demonstration that shames us out of violence, cannot account for a doorframe. Paul draws the line himself: “Christ our passover is sacrificed for us” (1Co 5:7).

The second thing is what happens when the two senses of the word are laid side by side. The posts of a house carried the blood and carried the law, and the posts on the road carried a king's summons to come and keep the passover, riding into a northern kingdom that mostly laughed at them — “they laughed them to scorn, and mocked them” (2Ch 30:10) — though some of Asher and Manasseh and Zebulun humbled themselves and came. That is preaching, exactly: a runner sent with a royal invitation to a sacrifice, mocked in most places and received in a few. Hezekiah sent the posts anyway.
roots_summary: Latin postis, a doorpost; Hebrew mezuzah (H4201), a doorpost; 'ayil (H352), a projecting pillar; rats (H7323), a runner; ratsats / ruts, to run.
roots_lines: Hebrew mezuzah (H4201) — a doorpost; the word behind the Jewish mezuzah fixed on the doorframe.
Hebrew mashqoph (H4947) — the lintel, the upper door post struck with blood (Exo 12:22).
Hebrew 'ayil (H352) — a post or pilaster of a gate; used of the temple doorposts in Ezekiel.
Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run; whence ratsim, the runners or posts who carried royal letters.
Hebrew pasach (H6452) — to pass over, to spare; the verb of Exo 12:13 and the root of Passover.
usage: “Strike it on the two side posts” — blood where the destroyer would see it.
“Write them upon the posts of thy house” — the law at the threshold.
“The posts went with the letters” — runners carrying a king's invitation.

pos: n. pl. (steps, journeyings, the course of a life — and in Micah, the eternal proceedings of the Son of God)
etymology: The verbal noun of go, Old English gan. In the KJV it renders Hebrew 'ashur and ma'gal, a step or track, and motsa'ah, a going forth or origin, and massa', a setting out on a journey.
biblical_def: Goings is the KJV's word for the whole course of a man's steps, and it is almost always used with a sense of who is holding him up. David prays, “Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not” (Psa 17:5), and testifies to the answer in the great deliverance psalm: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings” (Psa 40:2). Solomon adds the corresponding warning — a man's way is not private: “the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings” (Pro 5:21), said in the middle of a chapter about the strange woman, where a man is most inclined to imagine himself unobserved. Numbers uses the word for the stages of the wilderness march, which Moses was commanded to write down (Num 33:2) — a record of forty years of going out and going in. And then Micah takes the word out of time altogether. Prophesying the birthplace of the Messiah in a village too small to be reckoned among the thousands of Judah, he says of the ruler who will come from it: “whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” (Mic 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines goings as the act of moving, departure, or way of life and conduct; and in Scripture, the ways or doings of a person.
webster_full: GOING, n. The act of walking or moving; departure; pregnancy.
GOINGS, n. plu. Ways; doings; behavior; the course of a person's life.
In Scripture, the goings of a man are his steps or his whole conduct, which the Lord observes and directs.
The goings out and comings in of Israel in the wilderness were written by Moses at the commandment of the Lord.
Goings forth, in Micah v. 2, denotes the eternal generation and procession of the Messiah.
scriptures: Psa 17:5
Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not.
Psa 40:2
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.
Pro 5:21
For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.
Mic 5:2

But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
corruption_summary: Mic 5:2 is reduced to a prediction of a birthplace; the second half of the verse asserts the eternal pre-existence of the child, and Arianism in every century has had to get around it.
corruption_paragraphs: Mic 5:2 is quoted every December for its first half and rarely for its second, which is the doctrinally decisive one. A ruler is to come out of Bethlehem — and the same ruler's “goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.” The Hebrew miqqedem mime 'olam is as strong an expression of unbeginning existence as the language affords. The child who has a birthplace has no beginning. This is the doctrine the church confessed at Nicaea against Arius, that the Son is begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, and it is the doctrine every unitarian movement since — Arian, Socinian, and modern — has had to explain away. Micah puts the two natures in one verse, seven centuries early: born in a village, and going forth from everlasting.

The second thing in the word is a doctrine of guidance, and it corrects a common anxiety. Christians ask how to find God's will as though their steps were their own to arrange and the difficulty were locating a hidden map. David's language is different: he asks God to hold up his goings, and reports that God established them, and Solomon says God pondereth them — weighs and levels them. The same book says it flatly: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). The believer's duty is obedience in the plain commanded things; the ordering of the course belongs to God, and He has never mislaid it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ashur (H838), a step; ma'gal (H4570), a track or entrenchment; motsa'ah (H4163), a going forth, origin; massa' (H4550), a journey.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ashur (H838) — a step, a going; the word of Psa 17:5 and Psa 40:2.
Hebrew ma'gal (H4570) — a track, a wagon-rut, a course of life; the word of Pro 5:21.
Hebrew motsa'ah (H4163) — a going forth, an origin; the plural of Mic 5:2.
Hebrew miqqedem (H6924) — from of old, from aforetime; the first of Micah's two eternity terms.
Hebrew 'olam (H5769) — the vanishing point, everlasting, eternity; the second.
usage: “Hold up my goings in thy paths” — a prayer for the steps themselves.
“He pondereth all his goings” — a life weighed by God.
“Whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” — a child without a beginning.

pos: adj. (opposite, opposed, adverse — used of a headwind, of the flesh against the Spirit, of the law against the sinner, and of a nation walking against God)
etymology: From Latin contrarius, opposite, from contra, against. In the KJV it renders Hebrew qeri, a meeting in opposition or hostile encounter, and Greek enantios, over against, and hupenantios, set in opposition.
biblical_def: Contrary in Scripture is never a mild word. In Leviticus 26 it becomes the terrible refrain of the covenant curses: “if ye walk contrary unto me, and will not hearken unto me; I will bring seven times more plagues upon you according to your sins” (Lev 26:21) — and the chapter answers walking contrary with God Himself walking contrary, five times over, in escalating stages. Paul uses it of his own former life with painful candour: “I verily thought with myself, that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth” (Act 26:9) — conscience fully engaged, and pointed the wrong way. He uses it of the believer's divided experience: “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other” (Gal 5:17). And he uses it, most gloriously, of what the cross did with the law's indictment: “Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross” (Col 2:14). The Gospels keep the plain nautical sense: on the night He walked on the water, “the ship was now in the midst of the sea, tossed with waves: for the wind was contrary” (Mat 14:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contrary as opposite, adverse, repugnant; contradictory; and in navigation, unfavourable, as a contrary wind.
webster_full: CONTRARY, a. Opposite; adverse; moving against or in an opposite direction; as contrary winds.
Repugnant; contradictory; opposed to; as a doctrine contrary to Scripture.
Inconsistent; disagreeing; as a course of life contrary to the rules of virtue.
CONTRARY, n. A thing that is contrary or of opposite qualities; a proposition contrary to another.
On the contrary; in opposition; on the other side.
scriptures: And if ye walk contrary unto me, and will not hearken unto me; I will bring seven times more plagues upon you according to your sins.
Act 26:9
I verily thought with myself, that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
Gal 5:17
For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.
Col 2:14
Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;
corruption_summary: Sincerity is treated as its own justification; Paul says he sincerely thought he ought to act contrary to the name of Jesus, and calls himself for it the chief of sinners.
corruption_paragraphs: Act 26:9 is one of the most useful verses in Scripture against the modern doctrine that sincerity sanctifies. Paul is describing a period in which he was, by his own account, doing what his conscience told him he ought to do — and what he ought to do was hale men and women to prison and give his voice against them when they were put to death. He did it “ignorantly in unbelief” (1Ti 1:13), and he never once offers that as an excuse; he offers it as the reason he obtained mercy, and calls himself the chief of sinners in the same breath. A conscience is a real faculty and must not be violated, but it is not a standard; it must itself be bound by the word of God, or it will bind a man to the wrong duty with all the force of religious conviction.

Col 2:14 is the other side and the better news. The word contrary there describes a written indictment standing against the sinner — the cheirographon, a hand-written bond of debt with the debtor's own signature on it. Paul says it was blotted out, taken out of the way, and nailed to the cross. Not softened, not renegotiated, not offset by later obedience: cancelled, and the cancellation publicly posted where the debt was paid. That is why the divided experience of Gal 5:17 — flesh contrary to Spirit — is a war a believer fights from a position already secured. The contrariety within is real and lifelong; the contrariety of the law against him is finished.
roots_summary: Latin contra, against; Hebrew qeri (H7147), opposition, hostile encounter; Greek enantios (G1727), over against; hupenantios (G5227), set in opposition.
roots_lines: Hebrew qeri (H7147) — contrariness, hostile meeting; the refrain-word of Lev 26, used seven times.
Greek enantios (G1727) — opposite, contrary; of the wind in Mat 14:24, and of Paul's former mind.
Greek hupenantios (G5227) — set over against, adversary; the word for the bond in Col 2:14.
Greek cheirographon (G5498) — a handwriting, a bond of debt; what was nailed to the cross.
Greek antikeimai (G480) — to lie opposite, to oppose; the verb of Gal 5:17, flesh and Spirit in the field.
usage: “If ye walk contrary unto me” — the refrain of the covenant curses.
“I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus” — sincerity pointed the wrong way.
“Which was contrary to us… nailing it to his cross” — the indictment cancelled.

pos: v. (offended, made angry — used of God at David's sin and Israel's complaining, of Jonah at God's mercy, and of Christ at those who kept children away)
etymology: From Old French desplaisir, from Latin displicere, from dis-, apart, and placere, to please. In the KJV it renders Hebrew ra'a' be'eyne, to be evil in the eyes of, and Greek aganakteo, to be indignant.
biblical_def: Displeased is a quiet word for a serious thing, and the KJV uses it at four moments worth setting side by side. Twice it describes God. At the end of the chapter in which David took Bathsheba and had her husband killed, after the mourning, the marriage, and the birth, the writer adds one flat sentence: “But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD” (2Sa 11:27) — the whole affair had been managed to everyone's satisfaction, and heaven had not been consulted. And in the wilderness: “when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled” (Num 11:1) — grumbling is not a small sin, and fire fell in the uttermost parts of the camp. Once it describes a prophet displeased with God: “But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry” (Jon 4:1) — angry that Nineveh repented and was spared, which he had suspected all along would happen. And once it describes the Lord Jesus: “when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God” (Mar 10:14). It is the only place the Gospels use the word of Him, and the occasion was disciples turning away children.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines displease as to offend, to make angry in a slight degree, to disgust, and displeased as offended, disgusted, or vexed.
webster_full: DISPLEASE, v.t. To offend; to make angry, sometimes in a slight degree.
To disgust; to excite aversion in; as, sour things displease the taste.
To offend, as by an act contrary to the will or command of another.
DISPLEASED, pp. Offended; disgusted; vexed; provoked.
It is used of the Supreme Being after the manner of men, to signify his holy displeasure at sin.
scriptures: And when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house, and she became his wife, and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
Num 11:1

And when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp.
Jon 4:1
But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry.
But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Divine displeasure is either denied outright, as unworthy of a loving God, or reduced to a human mood; Scripture speaks of it plainly while the church confesses that God is without passions.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors gather around this word. The first says a God of love is never displeased, and treats the language of wrath as primitive residue. The second reads the language flatly and makes God a being of fluctuating moods who is upset and then consoled. The Reformed confession holds a narrower and better path. The 1689 Confession says God is “without body, parts, or passions” — He is not acted upon from outside, He does not swing from calm to fury, His displeasure at sin is not a disturbance that comes over Him. And yet it is entirely real: it is the eternal, settled, unchanging opposition of a holy nature to what is contrary to it, expressed in Scripture in language we can bear. The theological term is anthropopathism, and it is not a way of explaining the wrath away. It is a way of saying that God's displeasure is more certain than ours, not less, because it never varies with His temper.

The second thing here is the object of the only displeasure the Gospels attribute to the Lord Jesus. Not the crowds, not the Romans, not even the man with the withered hand's accusers — there He is grieved and angry, and the word is different. Here, in Mar 10:14, He is much displeased with His own disciples for keeping children away from Him, and He answers with a command and a doctrine: suffer them to come, forbid them not, for of such is the kingdom of God. Churches that make no room for children, and homes that treat catechising as optional, should sit with that verse a while. And note what David and the disciples have in common: both had arranged matters sensibly, and both had made an arrangement heaven disliked.
roots_summary: Latin displicere, to displease; Hebrew yera' be'eyne, to be evil in the eyes of; charah 'aph (H2734 + H639), the anger kindled; Greek aganakteo (G23), to be indignant.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'a' (H7489) — to be evil, displeasing; the idiom is literally “it was evil in the eyes of the LORD”.
Hebrew charah (H2734) — to burn, be kindled; used of anger, as in Num 11:1.
Hebrew 'aph (H639) — the nostril, and so anger; the Hebrew pictures wrath as hard breathing.
Greek aganakteo (G23) — to be indignant, much displeased; the word in Mar 10:14.
Greek orge (G3709) — settled wrath, as distinct from thumos, the boiling-over kind; God's wrath is orge.
usage: “The thing that David had done displeased the LORD” — one sentence after a chapter of scheming.
“When the people complained, it displeased the LORD” — grumbling reckoned as sin.
“He was much displeased… Suffer the little children” — the one occasion named of Christ.

pos: v. and adj. (thrown into confusion, put to shame, brought to nothing — the fate of Babel's builders and of every hope not set on God)
etymology: From Latin confundere, to pour together, mingle, from con-, together, and fundere, to pour. The KJV uses it for Hebrew bosh, to be ashamed, and balal, to mingle or confuse, and Greek kataischuno, to put to shame, and suncheo, to pour together.
biblical_def: Confounded carries two related senses in the Authorized Version and both begin at Babel. The first is literal mingling: “the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth” (Gen 11:9), and the name Babel is the pun on it. The second and far commoner sense is to be put to shame, to have one's expectation collapse in public. This is the great negative of the psalms of trust, and it is always used to say what will not happen to the man who trusts God: “They cried unto thee, and were delivered: they trusted in thee, and were not confounded” (Psa 22:5) — a verse from the psalm of the crucifixion, spoken by the Sufferer of the fathers who went before Him. Isaiah takes it into the everlasting: “Israel shall be saved in the LORD with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end” (Isa 45:17). And Peter gathers it up around the cornerstone: “Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded” (1Pe 2:6). There is one bright exception, where confusion serves the gospel: at Pentecost “the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6) — Babel running backwards.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confound as to mingle so that things cannot be distinguished; to perplex; to abash; to destroy; and confounded as mixed, perplexed, put to shame, or ruined.
webster_full: CONFOUND, v.t. To mingle and blend different things, so that their forms or natures cannot be distinguished.
To perplex; to disturb the apprehension by indistinctness of ideas or words.
To abash; to throw the mind into disorder; to cast down; to make ashamed.
To destroy; to bring to nought; to ruin; as, let them be confounded that seek my soul.
CONFOUNDED, pp. Mixed or blended in disorder; perplexed; abashed; put to shame and silence; astonished.
scriptures: Psa 22:5
They cried unto thee, and were delivered: they trusted in thee, and were not confounded.
But Israel shall be saved in the LORD with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end.
Act 2:6
Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.
Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.
corruption_summary: Shame is treated as a purely psychological injury to be dissolved by self-acceptance; Scripture treats it as a real objective condition before God, and answers it with an object outside the self.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic account of shame is that it is a distorted inner narrative, remedied by learning to accept oneself. Scripture's account is different in kind. To be confounded is to have staked something on a hope that then fails publicly — the idolater standing before an image that cannot save, the nation that trusted in Egypt watching Egypt's chariots break. The shame is not a misperception; it is an accurate reading of a real situation. Which is why the biblical remedy is never self-acceptance but a different object of trust. Every one of these verses is built the same way: he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. The cure for shame is a foundation that will hold, and the confidence is not in the strength of the believing but in the corner stone.

The second thing is the arc from Gen 11 to Act 2, which is one of the finest structures in Scripture. At Babel men built upward to make themselves a name, and God came down and confounded their speech so they could not understand one another, and scattered them. At Pentecost God came down again, and the multitude was confounded again — the Greek word is the same family — but this time because every man heard in his own tongue the wonderful works of God. The scattering is not reversed by everyone learning one language; the nations keep their tongues and hear the gospel in them. That is why translation has always been the church's instinct, and why the Revelation shows the redeemed out of every kindred and tongue rather than out of one.
roots_summary: Latin confundere, to pour together; Hebrew bosh (H954), to be ashamed; balal (H1101), to mingle, confuse; Greek kataischuno (G2617); suncheo (G4797).
roots_lines: Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mingle, confuse; the verb of Gen 11:9 and the pun behind the name Babel.
Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, disappointed; the commonest word rendered confounded.
Hebrew chapher (H2659) — to blush, be put to confusion; often paired with bosh.
Greek kataischuno (G2617) — to put to shame, dishonour; used in 1Pe 2:6 and Rom 5:5, “hope maketh not ashamed”.
Greek suncheo (G4797) — to pour together, confound; the word of the Pentecost crowd (Act 2:6).
usage: “They trusted in thee, and were not confounded” — the testimony of the fathers.
“Ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end” — shame ruled out forever.
“The multitude came together, and were confounded” — Babel running backwards.

pos: adj. (moving close to the ground — in the KJV a whole created order, “creeping thing”, blessed at creation, forbidden as food, and offered to Peter in a sheet)
etymology: From Old English creopan, to creep. It renders Hebrew remes and the verb ramas, to move about or glide, and sherets, a swarming thing; and Greek herpeton, a reptile, whence herpetology.
biblical_def: Creeping thing is one of Scripture's standing categories of animal life, alongside cattle, beasts of the field, and fowl of the air. It appears on the sixth day: “Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so” (Gen 1:24), and God saw that it was good. It goes into the ark by the same classification — “every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind” (Gen 7:14) — and fills the sea as well: “so is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable” (Psa 104:25). Under the law it becomes the plainest case of ceremonial uncleanness: “Whatsoever goeth upon the belly, and whatsoever goeth upon all four, or whatsoever hath more feet among all creeping things that creep upon the earth, them ye shall not eat; for they are an abomination” (Lev 11:42). Two New Testament passages turn on the category. Paul lists it at the bottom of the idolater's descent — the glory of God changed into an image like “birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things” (Rom 1:23). And Peter, on a housetop at Joppa, saw a sheet let down containing “all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air” (Act 10:12), and was told to rise, kill, and eat.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines creeping as moving with the belly to the ground, or with slow motion; and creeping thing, in Scripture, as any reptile or small animal that moves upon or near the ground.
webster_full: CREEP, v.i. To move with the belly on the ground, or the surface of any other body, as a worm or serpent.
To move slowly, feebly or timorously; as an old man creeps about the house.
To move secretly; to steal in; as, they creep into houses and lead captive silly women.
CREEPING, ppr. Moving on the belly, or with slow motion; stealing in insensibly.
Creeping thing, in the Scriptures, denotes the reptiles and lesser creatures that move upon the earth.
scriptures: Gen 1:24
And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so.
Gen 7:14

They, and every beast after his kind, and all the cattle after their kind, and every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind, and every fowl after his kind, every bird of every sort.

Whatsoever goeth upon the belly, and whatsoever goeth upon all four, or whatsoever hath more feet among all creeping things that creep upon the earth, them ye shall not eat; for they are an abomination.
Wherein were all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.
corruption_summary: The food laws are read as primitive hygiene or as arbitrary taboo; Scripture gives them a stated purpose — to teach a separated people to distinguish — and then declares them fulfilled and abolished in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Two explanations of Lev 11 miss it. The hygienic reading says the unclean animals carried disease, which fails on the details — the rabbit and the camel are not notably dangerous, and the law is not framed as health advice. The arbitrary-taboo reading says the categories are meaningless boundary markers. Scripture supplies its own reason, and it is neither: “I am the LORD your God, which have separated you from other people. Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean” (Lev 20:24-25). The dietary law was a daily, three-times-a-day drill in the doctrine of separation, taught at the table where it could not be forgotten. A people who could not eat like the nations would not easily forget that they were not the nations.

And that is exactly why the sheet at Joppa mattered so much, and why Peter said “Not so, Lord” to a direct command. The vision was repeated three times and answered with a declaration — “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Act 10:15) — and Peter himself gives the interpretation when he walks into a Gentile house: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Act 10:28). The ceremonial law was a shadow whose substance is Christ, and it is fulfilled and set aside in Him; the moral law of the ten commandments is not, and remains binding. Mark states the conclusion flatly of our Lord's own teaching: “purging all meats” (Mar 7:19). The creeping things of the sheet were the sign that the middle wall of partition was coming down.
roots_summary: Old English creopan; Hebrew remes (H7431), creeping things, from ramas (H7430), to glide about; sherets (H8318), a swarming thing; Greek herpeton (G2062).
roots_lines: Hebrew remes (H7431) — creeping things; a collective noun for the small life that moves on the ground.
Hebrew ramas (H7430) — to glide, move about, creep; the verb of Gen 1:26 and Psa 104:20.
Hebrew sherets (H8318) — a swarm, teeming creature; the word of the swarming things of Lev 11.
Hebrew gachon (H1512) — the belly; “whatsoever goeth upon the belly”, echoing the curse on the serpent (Gen 3:14).
Greek herpeton (G2062) — a creeping thing, reptile; used in Act 10:12 and Rom 1:23.
usage: “Cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth” — a created order God called good.
“Them ye shall not eat; for they are an abomination” — a daily drill in separation.
“Wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air” — the sheet at Joppa.
